findings.text: TD VM initialization marks the VM as having protected state, protected EOI handling, private memory and protected performance monitoring, opts out of guest PAT handling, points MMIO handling at guest-delivered virtualization exceptions, clamps allowed vCPU count to present CPUs, and leaves trust-domain state uninitialized.
For TDX the MMIO shadow entry is cleared so permission checks fault and the fault is delivered to the guest for conversion into a hypercall, instead of causing a misconfiguration exit.
TDX vCPU maximum is the lesser of the generic KVM maximum and the number of present logical CPUs, avoiding direct exposure of a module-wide limit that would vary across platforms.
Conversion from generic VM object to TDX-specific container derives the enclosing structure from its embedded generic member.

VMX VM initialization disables pause exits when the paravirtual pause gap is unset, emits one-time warnings when starting under system L1TF exposure with extended page tables while multithreading is active or flush mitigation is off, and sizes per-CPU dirty logging when page-modification logging is enabled.

Virtualization-technology VM teardown dispatches on trust-domain membership: protected guests release the encryption key during pre-destroy and reclaim trust-domain pages during destroy, while conventional guests use the VMX destroy path.

Encryption-key release first returns when no key is assigned, then takes CPU and module locks, flushes each virtual processor on its current CPU, completes virtual-processor flush bookkeeping, performs package-aware cache writeback on online CPUs, frees the key identifier, and releases the key slot.

Key release holds the CPU hotplug read lock across per-vCPU flushing and cache writeback, and serializes module-wide flush-done plus key-free operations with a dedicated mutex to avoid busy contention between concurrent guest destructions.

If virtual-processor flush completion or key-free reports an unexpected module error, the key identifier is intentionally leaked and an error is logged; a not-done flush status exits early without freeing.
A key identifier counts as assigned only when positive; freeing returns the identifier to the key allocator, marks the slot unassigned, and drops the associated misc-cgroup charge and reference.
Per-vCPU flush is skipped when the vCPU has no host CPU association; otherwise it synchronously invokes a remote flush routine on that CPU and checks the module return status.

Trust-domain lifecycle starts uninitialized at VM creation, must reach initialized before a TDX vCPU can be created, and returns to uninitialized after VM destroy; TDX vCPUs likewise start uninitialized at creation and return there after their pages are reclaimed.

Trust-domain control-page reclamation is skipped while a key remains assigned; otherwise it reclaims each control-structure page in the saved array, frees the array, reclaims the domain root page, flushes caches for that root, resets quirks, and frees the root.
Any control-page reclaim failure leaks that page because the host can no longer safely reuse it; root-page failure aborts further teardown.
VMX VM destruction releases the posted-interrupt descriptor table using an allocation order computed from the maximum vCPU identifier count.
Posted-interrupt table order is the page order for an array with one entry per possible vCPU identifier.

vCPU precreation for conventional guests ensures a zeroed posted-interrupt table exists only when an in-kernel interrupt chip and posted-interrupt virtualization are active; it is idempotent and reports allocation failure.

vCPU creation dispatches on trust-domain membership; TDX creation rejects uninitialized domains and non-split interrupt-chip configurations, then establishes confidential floating-point state, protected local-APIC state, default firmware-visible controls, protected timekeeping snapshots, conditional state protection, and a posted-interrupt descriptor with notification suppression.

TDX vCPUs start with system-call, long-mode and no-execute enabled, automatic debug-register switching, fully guest-owned low control registers, immutable time offset and scaling snapshots, tile-aware intercept relaxation when the domain enables tile state, and a dedicated posted-interrupt vector.

VMX vCPU creation acquires a virtual-processor identifier, an optional zeroed page-modification log page, default all-ones user-return register masks with special handling for transactional-memory control, a cleared VM control structure with optional enlightened MSR-bitmap support, plus on-demand APIC-access, real-mode identity, conversion-error and posted-interrupt resources; each failure step releases what was already acquired.

A loaded VM control structure bundles the control page, optional shadow page, owning CPU, launch flag, optional deny-by-default MSR bitmap, host state and shadowed controls; allocation zeroes the page, stamps the appropriate revision, and marks shadow pages distinctly.
APIC-access virtualization is required only with flexpriority plus in-kernel APIC; posted-interrupt virtualization is usable only with in-kernel APIC plus the feature enabled.

Real-mode identity setup is serialized by the slot mutex with a done flag for once-only installation; virtual-processor identifier allocation and release serialize bitmap updates with a dedicated spinlock.

Identity mapping installs a single private page at a fixed guest address and fills it with present writable user huge-page entries forming a one-to-one mapping, failing if the slot cannot be created or the entries cannot be copied.
Identifier zero means virtual-processor identifiers disabled or exhausted; allocation returns the first clear position under lock and release clears the indicated position unless disabled or zero.

vCPU teardown dispatches on trust-domain membership; TDX teardown flushes and returns early while still associated with a CPU, otherwise reclaims virtual-processor control pages unless a key remains assigned, while VMX teardown releases logging, identifier, nested, control-structure, conversion-error and posted-interrupt resources and clears the table entry.

Nested teardown brings the vCPU online, synthesizes an exit to leave guest mode and clears pending state when active, then resets virtualization-on state, frees the secondary identifier, tears down shadow and cached control structures, releases pages, roots and enlightened state, and frees the secondary control structure.
Disabling shadow control structures clears the corresponding secondary execution control, invalidates the link pointer, and drops the pending synchronization flag.

vCPU reset dispatches on trust-domain membership; TDX reset warns if asked to handle INIT, which is unsupported, and otherwise leaves initialization to a later userspace configuration call that defines the vCPU model.

Sentinel minus one marks an unassigned encryption key, an unassociated host CPU, an unassigned control-structure owner, and an invalid nested posted-interrupt target; zero marks a disabled or exhausted virtual-processor identifier and a cleared posted-interrupt table entry.
TDX uses a cleared MMIO shadow entry to request fault plus guest-delivered virtualization exception; page-modification logging and conversion-error buffers each occupy a single zeroed page.

TDX VM state combines lifecycle state, encryption key, cgroup handle, timekeeping snapshots, feature masks, and a domain descriptor with control-structure page array plus counts and a root page; TDX vCPU state combines lifecycle state, virtual-processor descriptor with control-page array plus root page and address, and a posted-interrupt descriptor with wakeup linkage.

Module-error helpers capture the failing operation name with optional extra status words for diagnostics; reclaim paths treat unexpected module errors as fatal for that page or key while explicitly ignoring busy contention where teardown ordering precludes it.
Page-modification log teardown is idempotent: it frees the log page only when present and clears the pointer.
